title: SBA Lender Service Provider: What It Is, the Rules, and How Lenders Scale With One
summary: An SBA lender service provider does lender work on SBA loans for pay from the lender. SBA reviews each agreement, and the lender stays fully responsible.
body_markdown:
An SBA lender service provider (LSP) is an agent paid by the lender to perform lender functions on a specific SBA loan or portfolio. Those functions are originating, disbursing, servicing, or liquidating the loan. SBA decides LSP status loan by loan, and the lender stays fully responsible for the loan.


SBA's regulations in the[13 CFR 103.1 definitions](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-13/chapter-I/part-103/section-103.1) describe an LSP as an agent who "carries out lender functions" for "compensation from the lender." The same SBA section adds that SBA decides who counts as an LSP "on a loan-by-loan basis." A vendor can't simply pick the label for itself.


For an SBA approved lender, an LSP is also an operating-model choice. It decides who handles intake, documents, closing, servicing, and workouts, and how many people the lender needs on staff. SBA lending teams usually weigh three models: build in-house, outsource to an LSP, or run the work on a technology platform.


‍


### LSPs vs. packagers vs. referral agents


SBA's regulations define three types of agents that lenders and borrowers often mix up. The difference comes down to who the agent works for, who pays, and what work it performs. SBA sets LSP and packager status loan by loan, so a firm's role can change from one loan to the next.


Lender service provider SBA loan packager Referral agent


Works for The lender The applicant or the lender The applicant or the lender


Who pays The lender only The applicant or the lender The applicant or the lender


What it does Performs lender functions: origination, disbursement, servicing, or liquidation Prepares the applicant's SBA loan application Refers an applicant to a lender, or a lender to an applicant


Form 159 treatment (7(a)) Not required for LSP services under an SBA-reviewed LSP agreement Required Required


A packager's work ends with the application, and a referral agent's work ends with the introduction. An LSP keeps working inside the lender's process after that point. SBA reviews the LSP's written agreement with the lender, which is why Form 159 isn't required for those LSP services.


‍


### How SBA loan programs shape LSP work


SBA's[SBA 7(a) loan program](https://www.sba.gov/funding-programs/loans/7a-loans) page states that the maximum 7(a) loan amount is $5 million. The LSP rules discussed in this guide come from SBA's SOP 50 10 8.1, effective Oct 1, 2026, for 7(a) loans.


The program runs at real scale. SBA's[SBA FY2025 lending results](https://www.sba.gov/article/2025/09/30/trump-sba-delivers-record-capital-small-businesses-fy25) reported 77,600 7(a) loans for $37 billion and 6,750 504 loans for $7.8 billion. At that volume, every manual step in intake, closing, and servicing repeats across thousands of files.


The 7(a) LSP agreement framework discussed here applies to 7(a) loans, and 504 arrangements differ. Lenders that run both programs should confirm which rules govern each relationship.


‍


### Where an LSP fits in the SBA loan lifecycle


The 13 CFR 103.1 definition names four lender functions: originating, disbursing, servicing, and liquidating. An LSP can take on one, several, or all four for a given loan or portfolio.


Each function carries a different workload and a different risk profile. Mapping them helps a lender decide what to keep in-house, what to outsource, and what to automate. The sections below walk through each stage in loan order.


#### Origination and intake


**42% faster speed to funding (Lendflow platform data).** According to Lendflow platform data, pre-qualified offers hosted on Lendflow drive an average of 42% faster speed to funding. Lendflow platform data also shows its embedded finance customers operate with 80% smaller teams while converting similar funding volumes.


Origination is where manual work piles up first. It covers application intake, document collection, and constant back-and-forth with the borrower. In SBA origination, a missing tax return or an unsigned form can stall a file for days.


Borrower experience matters here, and a separate, independent data source shows why. The Federal Reserve Banks'[Small Business Credit Survey](https://www.fedsmallbusiness.org/reports/survey/2026/2026-report-on-employer-firms) found that 42% of applicants received the full financing they sought, and 22% received none. The survey covers small employer firms across all lender types, so it isn't specific to SBA borrowers or Lendflow customers.


Skip manual file review—Lendflow's Doc Analyzer provides[automated loan document analysis](https://www.lendflow.com/solutions/doc-analyzer) as documents arrive. The Borrower Platform gives applicants one unified place to apply and upload. AI communications tools handle status updates and document requests, saving lenders hours of follow-up.


#### Underwriting, closing, and disbursement


After intake, an LSP may support credit analysis, assemble closing packages, and manage disbursement steps. Under SOP 50 10 8.1, the 7(a) lender, not the LSP, bears full responsibility for its SBA loan operation.


One detail matters for lenders buying software. Under SOP 50 10 8.1, technology vendors whose services include underwriting are considered LSPs. They must work under an SBA-reviewed LSP agreement, which the compliance section below covers in detail.


Skip re-keying data between systems—Lendflow Automate delivers[AI-powered lending operations](https://www.lendflow.com/lendflow-automate) across closing workflows. It automates document handling, communication, and decision support. That keeps closing teams lean as volume grows.


#### Servicing and liquidation


After funding, an LSP can handle ongoing SBA loan servicing. That includes payment handling, borrower communication, and workouts for struggling loans. If a loan defaults, the LSP can manage liquidation on the lender's behalf, within the scope the agreement sets.


Servicing runs for the life of the loan, so headcount can grow quietly here. Lendflow's guide on how to[grow SBA deal flow](https://www.lendflow.com/post/how-sba-lenders-can-grow-deal-flow-without-adding-operational-overhead) explains how lenders add volume without adding operational overhead.


The agreement should spell out which servicing and liquidation tasks the LSP performs. It also can't hand the LSP power of attorney or any share of loan risk. The next section covers those limits.


‍


### Compliance rules every SBA lender service provider must follow


The rules come from 13 CFR Part 103 and SBA's SOP 50 10 8.1, effective Oct 1, 2026. SOP 50 10 8.1 replaces SOP 50 10 8 and applies to 7(a) loans numbered on or after that date.


This section is informational and isn't legal advice. Have compliance counsel review any LSP agreement before you sign it or submit it to SBA.


#### Written agreements reviewed by SBA


SBA's[written LSP agreement rules](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-13/chapter-I/part-103/section-103.5) in 13 CFR 103.5 require each LSP to "enter into a written agreement with each lender" it serves. The same section states that "SBA will review all such agreements." Every lender relationship needs its own agreement.


Under SOP 50 10 8.1, lenders submit each LSP agreement to SBA's Loan Guaranty Processing Center (LGPC) for review. Lenders may send agreements toLSPagreements@sba.gov . If the agreement changes after SBA's review, the lender must submit the revised version for review.


Every LSP agreement must also respect four firm limits. Each limit below names its source:


- Under SOP 50 10 8.1, the agreement can't grant the LSP power of attorney to act for the lender.
- Under both 13 CFR 103.5 and SOP 50 10 8.1, the lender and the LSP can't share in any secondary market premium.
- Under SOP 50 10 8.1, the LSP can't assume any risk on the unguaranteed portion of a loan.
- Under SOP 50 10 8.1, the LSP must be located in the United States, its territories, or possessions.


#### Compensation, Form 159, and lender responsibility


An LSP may only receive compensation from the 7(a) lender for services under an SBA-reviewed agreement. Those charges can't be passed on to the applicant or paid out of SBA-guaranteed loan proceeds. Within those limits, 13 CFR 103.5 gives lenders reasonable discretion in setting LSP compensation.


SBA reviews the LSP agreement, so SBA Form 159 isn't required for the services the LSP provides under that reviewed agreement. Form 159 is still required for agents outside a reviewed LSP agreement, such as packagers and referral agents. That applies whether the applicant or the lender pays them.


SBA's[SOP 50 10 LSP requirements](https://www.sba.gov/document/sop-50-10-lender-development-company-loan-programs) state that "the 7(a) Lender itself, not the LSP, bears full responsibility" for its SBA loan operation. SBA also expects lenders to exercise due diligence and prudent oversight of third-party vendors, including LSPs. Lenders should build reporting, audit access, and performance reviews into every LSP relationship.


Outsourcing the work leaves the accountability with the lender. Track LSP performance with the same metrics used for internal teams, such as file completeness, turnaround time, and exception rates.


#### When technology vendors count as LSPs


SOP 50 10 8.1 addresses a point many lenders overlook. It states that "entities providing technology services that include underwriting are considered to be LSPs." Those vendors must provide their services under an SBA-reviewed LSP agreement.


This matters for any lender evaluating AI underwriting or automated decisioning software. The test turns on function. If the software performs underwriting, SBA treats the vendor as an LSP, whatever the vendor calls itself.


Document the answer for every tool in your stack, including intake widgets and decisioning engines. A written map of who performs each lender function makes LSP agreement reviews and vendor oversight easier to manage. It also gives examiners and counsel a clear record of where each decision happens.


Before signing, ask each vendor which functions its product performs and whether it will sign an LSP agreement for SBA review. Lendflow's guide to[AI underwriting for SBA lenders](https://www.lendflow.com/post/ai-underwriting-tools-for-sba-lenders-how-to-choose-one-that-speeds-decisions-without-adding-risk) covers how to choose tools that speed decisions without adding risk.

### How to choose an SBA lender service provider or technology partner


**$1.5B+ in offers.** More than $1.5 billion in offers were made on Lendflow's platform in the 12 months through March 2025. According to Lendflow platform data, its embedded finance customers run with 80% smaller teams while converting similar funding volumes.


Scale without growing overhead—automate the work that would otherwise need new hires. SBA lending companies differ widely in which functions they cover and how they report. Use this checklist to compare LSPs and technology partners side by side.


Criterion What to ask Why it matters


Scope of functions Which of origination, disbursement, servicing, and liquidation does the partner perform? Scope decides whether an SBA-reviewed LSP agreement is needed


Agreement readiness Will the partner sign a written LSP agreement, resubmit revisions, and confirm it is US-based? SBA reviews all LSP agreements, including revised ones


Oversight and reporting What reports, audit access, and performance metrics does the partner provide? The lender keeps full responsibility and must oversee vendors


Data and integrations Does it connect to your systems and data providers through APIs? Fragmented systems create data silos and rework


Document automation How does it collect, analyze, and flag borrower documents? Manual document review grows headcount as volume grows


Borrower experience Do borrowers get one place to apply, upload, and track status? Friction shows up as incomplete files and follow-up calls


Cost model Is pricing per loan, per function, or platform-based, and is it lender-paid only? LSP fees can't pass to the borrower or come from guaranteed proceeds


The second decision is the operating model. Each option below leaves the lender fully responsible for its SBA loan operation.


In-house team Outsourced LSP Technology platform


Control Full, with internal staff Shared through the written agreement Full, with automated workflows


How it scales Add headcount as volume grows Expand LSP scope under the agreement Automate tasks so teams stay lean


SBA agreement review Not needed for internal staff Required for the LSP agreement Required if the platform includes underwriting

### FAQs


#### What does an SBA lender service provider do?


An SBA lender service provider performs lender functions, such as originating, disbursing, servicing, or liquidating SBA loans, for compensation from the lender. SBA decides LSP status loan by loan.


#### Is an SBA loan packager the same as a lender service provider?


No, a packager prepares the applicant's SBA loan application and can be paid by the applicant or the lender. An LSP performs lender functions for the lender under an SBA-reviewed agreement.


#### Who pays an SBA lender service provider?


Only the lender pays an LSP for services under an SBA-reviewed agreement. Those fees can't be charged to the borrower or paid from SBA-guaranteed loan proceeds.


#### Does SBA approve lender service providers?


SBA reviews LSP agreements, which lenders submit to the Loan Guaranty Processing Center, and it decides LSP status loan by loan. The lender remains fully responsible for its SBA loan operation.


#### What is the 20% rule for SBA loans?


Under SBA's[20 percent guarantee rule](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-13/section-120.160) in 13 CFR 120.160, holders of at least a 20% ownership interest generally must guarantee the loan. SBA or a delegated lender may also require guarantees from other individuals or entities, whatever their ownership share.
